sections.title: Lesson 9.1: The Business Cycle
sections.overview: The business cycle describes the regular fluctuation of the economy through four phases: expansion, peak, contraction, and trough. Understanding these phases, the indicators used to measure them, and how industries respond to them is foundational to fundamental analysis and making suitable recommendations. This lesson also introduces the balance sheet and income statement as tools to evaluate corporate financial health.
key_concepts: Four phases of the business cycle: Expansion → Peak → Contraction → Trough → (back to Expansion).
Expansion: rising consumer demand, rising industrial production, rising stock prices, rising property values, increasing GDP.

Peak (prosperity): very low unemployment, slowdown in inflation growth, slowing GDP growth, steady consumer demand. Inflation pressure is typically highest near/during expansion as productive capacity is fully utilized.
Contraction: rising bankruptcies and bond defaults, higher consumer debt, falling stock prices, rising inventories, decreasing GDP.
Trough: high unemployment, flat GDP, low but no longer decreasing consumer demand.
Recession: contraction lasting six months (two consecutive quarters of declining GDP) or longer.
Depression: contraction lasting 18 months or longer.
Some economists split expansion into 'recovery' (trough back to prior peak) and 'expansion' (growth beyond prior peak).
GDP: total value of all goods/services produced within U.S. borders (regardless of nationality of producer); released quarterly by Commerce Department.
GNP: total output of U.S. citizens/entities wherever produced (domestic or abroad).
Real GDP = GDP adjusted for inflation using CPI (constant-dollar measure).
CPI: Consumer Price Index — primary measure of inflation/deflation, computed monthly on a basket of consumer prices.

Leading indicators (predict future direction): M2 money supply, building permits/housing starts, initial unemployment claims, average manufacturing workweek, new orders for consumer goods, machine tool orders, changes in inventories of durable goods, sensitive materials prices, S&P 500 stock prices, changes in business/consumer borrowing.
Coincident indicators (move with economy): hours worked, employment levels, nonagricultural employment, personal income, industrial production, manufacturing and trade sales, GDP.

Lagging indicators (confirm trends): corporate profits, average duration of unemployment, labor cost per unit of output, inventory-to-sales ratio, commercial/industrial loans outstanding, consumer installment credit-to-personal-income ratio.

Price movement terminology: Inflation (general rise), Deflation (general decline, often during recession), Stagnation (slow growth + high unemployment), Hyperinflation (extreme accelerating inflation), Stagflation (inflation + high unemployment simultaneously).
Cyclical industries: sensitive to business cycle; produce durable/capital goods and raw materials (steel, autos, heavy equipment, washers/dryers).
Noncyclical (defensive) industries: relatively unaffected by cycle; produce nondurable consumables (food, utilities, clothing, drugs/pharma, tobacco, liquor).
Countercyclical industries: tend to rise when economy falls; classic example is gold/precious metals mining and refining.
Growth industries: appear disconnected from cycle, grow regardless of economy (until they mature).
Special situations: company- or industry-specific events (hostile takeover, technological/cultural shift) creating unusual profit potential or downside risk.
Balance Sheet: snapshot of financial position at a point in time; Assets = Liabilities + Net Worth.
Asset categories: Current assets (cash, securities, receivables, inventory), Fixed assets (real estate, equipment, furniture), Other/Intangible (goodwill, trademarks, copyrights).
Liability categories: Current liabilities (due within 12 months — accounts payable, accrued wages, accrued taxes, current interest), Long-term liabilities (notes, bonds).
Net Worth components: Preferred stock, Common stock (at par), Capital in excess of par (paid-in surplus), Retained earnings.
Income Statement (P&L): summarizes revenues and expenses over a fiscal period; measures profitability.

Income Statement flow: Net Sales − COGS − Operating Costs (incl. depreciation) = Operating Profit; + Nonoperating Income = EBIT; − Interest = Pretax Income; − Taxes = Net Income; − Preferred Dividends = Earnings Available to Common; − Common Dividends = Retained Earnings.
rules: GDP figures are released quarterly by the U.S. Commerce Department.
CPI is computed monthly and is used to convert nominal GDP to real GDP.
Recession threshold (exam definition): two consecutive quarters (six months) of declining GDP.
formulas: Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities (dollar amount)
Current Ratio = Current Assets / Current Liabilities
Acid-Test (Quick) Ratio = (Current Assets − Inventory) / Current Liabilities
Debt Ratio = Long-Term Debt / (Long-Term Debt + Net Worth)
EPS = Earnings Available to Common / Common Shares Outstanding
P/E Ratio = Current Market Value (Price) / EPS
Real GDP = Nominal GDP adjusted by CPI
mnemonics: Cycle order: 'Every Person Can Trough' — Expansion, Peak, Contraction, Trough.
Defensive = things you consume DAILY: Food, Drugs, Tobacco, Liquor, Utilities, Clothing (FUDD-LC).
Cyclical = BIG, HEAVY, DURABLE (steel, autos, capital goods).
Counter = GOLD goes UP when economy goes DOWN.
Leading indicators 'lead' — think Stock prices (S&P 500), housing permits, M2.
Lagging = 'Last' — corporate profits, duration of unemployment.

sections.title: Lesson 9.2: Economic Theories and International Trade
sections.overview: Fiscal policy is set by Congress and the President through taxation and spending decisions; monetary policy is set by the Federal Reserve. Two competing fiscal theories—Keynesian (demand-side) and supply-side—offer different prescriptions for government involvement. International trade is shaped by exchange rates, which directly affect the balance of trade and balance of payments.
key_concepts: Fiscal policy = government taxation and spending decisions (Congress + President).
Monetary policy = money-supply and interest-rate decisions (Federal Reserve).
Keynesian (Demand-Side) Theory: John Maynard Keynes; government should actively manage demand through spending and taxation.
Keynesian logic: Lower taxes/higher government spending → more disposable income → more demand → economic growth. Higher taxes/lower spending → cools demand → controls inflation.
Supply-Side Theory: government should reduce taxes and regulatory burden on businesses; let market forces determine prices and output. Associated with Arthur Laffer.
Monetarist Theory: Milton Friedman; controlling the money supply is the key to economic stability — foundation of Federal Reserve policy.
Both demand-side and supply-side agree that LOWER TAXES encourage economic activity; they differ on the role/size of government spending.
Exchange Rate: relative value of one currency vs. another.
Strong U.S. dollar → U.S. exports become more expensive abroad (exports fall); foreign imports become cheaper in U.S. (imports rise); helps keep U.S. inflation in check.
Weak U.S. dollar → U.S. exports cheaper abroad (exports rise); imports more expensive in U.S. (imports fall); tends to increase U.S. inflation.
Balance of Payments: total flow of money between U.S. and foreign nations; surplus = net inflow, deficit = net outflow.
Balance of Trade: largest component of balance of payments — exports vs. imports of goods.
Credit items (money flowing IN): U.S. exports, foreign spending in the U.S., foreign investment in U.S.
Debit items (money flowing OUT): U.S. imports, U.S. investments abroad, U.S. bank loans abroad, U.S. foreign aid.
High foreign interest rates pull capital OUT of the U.S. (deficit pressure); high U.S. rates attract foreign capital IN (surplus pressure).
rules: Fiscal policy authority: Congress and the President — NOT the Federal Reserve.
Monetary policy authority: Federal Reserve Board — NOT Congress.
formulas: Balance of Payments = Credits (money in) − Debits (money out)
mnemonics: Keynes = 'K' for Kongress/spending — government Knows best.
Monetarist = Money supply (Friedman) — basis of Fed action.
Strong dollar = Strong buying power abroad → imports IN, exports OUT (weak).
Weak dollar = Weak buying power abroad → exports STRONG, imports weak.

sections.title: Lesson 9.3: The Federal Reserve and Monetary Policy
sections.overview: The Federal Reserve Board (FRB), established by the Federal Reserve Act of 1913, is the U.S. central bank. Its dual mandate is to promote maximum employment and stable prices (control inflation). The Fed uses diagnostic tools (money supply measures M1, M2, M3) and active tools (open-market operations, the discount rate, IORB, Regulation T) to manage the money supply. Four key interest rates anchor the cost of money in the U.S. economy.
key_concepts: Federal Reserve Act of 1913 created the Federal Reserve System (12 regional Federal Reserve Banks + member national/state banks).
FRB dual mandate: (1) maximum employment, (2) stable prices / controlled inflation.
FOMC (Federal Open Market Committee): directs open-market operations; consists of 7 Board Governors + NY Fed President + 4 rotating regional Fed presidents.
Monetarist Milton Friedman's theories underlie much of Fed policy.
Diagnostic Tools — Money Supply Measures:
M1 = currency in circulation + demand deposits (checking accounts) — most liquid.
M2 = M1 + consumer savings deposits (savings accounts, retail/nonnegotiable CDs, money market funds, overnight repos).
M3 = M2 + large time deposits (jumbo/negotiable CDs, multi-day repos).
M1 ⊂ M2 ⊂ M3 — moving funds within the hierarchy does not change the larger measure.
Active Tools of the Fed:

(1) Open-Market Operations (most frequently used): FOMC buys/sells U.S. Treasury securities. BUY = money INTO economy, supply UP, rates DOWN, economy expands. SELL = money OUT of economy, supply DOWN, rates UP, economy contracts.

(2) Discount Rate: rate the Fed charges member banks for short-term loans (often via repos). Lower rate = ease; Higher rate = tighten. It is the only one of the four key rates set by a government body.

(3) Reserve Requirement: historically, the percentage of deposits banks must hold in reserve. **IMPORTANT UPDATE: The Fed reduced the reserve requirement ratio to 0% effective March 26, 2020, and it remains at 0%.** Reserve requirements are no longer an active policy tool.

(4) Interest on Reserve Balances (IORB): the Fed pays interest on bank reserves held at the Fed. IORB is now the principal policy rate tool, functioning as the floor of the federal funds target range corridor (replaced the former IOER).
(5) Regulation T: sets the initial margin deposit (currently 50% since 1974); rarely changed in practice.
Four Prominent Interest Rates:
Federal Funds Rate: rate commercial money-center banks charge each other for overnight loans of $1 million+. Most volatile; set by the market (not the Fed directly, though Fed targets a range).
Prime Rate: rate large commercial banks charge their most creditworthy corporate customers for unsecured loans. Set by each bank.

Broker Call Loan Rate (Call Money Rate): rate banks charge broker-dealers on loans used to finance customer margin accounts. Typically ~1% above other short-term rates. Callable on 24-hour notice. Set by the lending bank.
Discount Rate: rate Fed charges member banks. Set by the Federal Reserve (the only one of the four set by the government).
Easy Money Policy (stimulate economy): BUY securities, LOWER discount rate, (historically) lower reserve requirement.
Tight Money Policy (cool economy/fight inflation): SELL securities, RAISE discount rate, (historically) raise reserve requirement.
rules: Federal Reserve Act of 1913 — establishes the Federal Reserve System.
Regulation T (FRB) — current initial margin requirement: 50% of purchase price (unchanged since 1974).
Reserve requirement ratio = 0% effective March 26, 2020 (Federal Reserve action; still 0% as of 2026). Reserve requirements should NOT be cited as an active modern Fed tool.
Open-market operations are the Fed's most frequently used active tool.
formulas: Easy Money: Fed BUYS securities → Money Supply ↑ → Interest Rates ↓ → Economy ↑
Tight Money: Fed SELLS securities → Money Supply ↓ → Interest Rates ↑ → Economy ↓
M2 + Large Time Deposits (jumbo CDs, multi-day repos) = M3
mnemonics: 'BLEED' for Easy Money: BUY securities, LOWER discount rate, EASE conditions, Economy Expands, Demand grows.
'STRIP' for Tight Money: SELL securities, Tighten, Raise rates, Inflation Prevented.
M1 = Money you can spend Immediately (cash + checking).
M2 = M1 + Mid-liquidity Money (savings, MMF, retail CDs).
Discount rate is the ONLY rate set by the GOVERNMENT — the other three are set by the lender (bank).
Four rates from most volatile/short to anchor: Fed Funds → Broker Call → Prime → Discount.
